findings.issue_text: parseRefreshTokenResponse.ts:8-10 — `[z.string().toString()]` and `[z.string().optional().toString()]` both stringify to the key `"[object Object]"`, so the second key overwrites the first and minimumTokenResponseSchema only validates `access_token`, never the expiry field
parseRefreshTokenResponse.ts:8-10 — the schema silently strips all other properties (expiry, scope, instance_url) from the parsed result that callers then persist

parseRefreshTokenResponse.ts:22-24 — when the response has no `refresh_token`, the literal string `"refresh_token"` is injected and returned, so callers (Office365 CalendarService.ts:262, zoom) persist the placeholder into `credential.key`, destroying the real refresh token and breaking the integration

refreshOAuthTokens.ts:6-16 — in sync mode the function returns a raw fetch `Response` while callers (googlecalendar CalendarService.ts:86 `res?.data`, zoho-bigin:85 and zohocrm:204 `tokenInfo.data.error`, hubspot:177 typed as HubspotToken) expect provider-specific/axios shapes, causing TypeError or undefined reads when credential sync is enabled

zoho-bigin/lib/CalendarService.ts:93 — passes `credentialId` instead of `credential.userId`, so the sync endpoint receives a credential ID as `calcomUserId` and refreshes/returns tokens for the wrong or non-existent user

salesforce/lib/CalendarService.ts:75-97 — unconditional token refresh plus `prisma.credential.update` on every SalesforceCalendarService construction regardless of access token validity, adding a network round-trip and DB write per instantiation and risking Salesforce refresh rate limits

salesforce/lib/CalendarService.ts:86 — `if (response.statusText !== "OK")` is an unreliable success check since statusText is empty on HTTP/2 and many fetch implementations, causing successful refreshes to throw; should use `response.ok`/`response.status`

salesforce/lib/CalendarService.ts:91-93 — `if (!accessTokenParsed.success)` is dead code because parseRefreshTokenResponse already throws on failure, and it is a latent trap for future callers relying on `.success`

apps/web/pages/api/webhook/app-credential.ts:22-27 — webhook secret compared with `!==` rather than a constant-time comparison, leaking the secret to a timing oracle on an endpoint that writes arbitrary OAuth credentials; use crypto.timingSafeEqual

apps/web/pages/api/webhook/app-credential.ts:29 — `schema.parse(req.body)` throws an unhandled ZodError producing a 500 and unhandled rejection instead of a 400 for malformed input; same for `JSON.parse(symmetricDecrypt(...))` at line 52 with a wrong encryption key

apps/web/pages/api/webhook/app-credential.ts:16 — no HTTP method check, so GET/DELETE and other methods fall through to credential mutation, unlike every other handler which gates on method via defaultHandler

office365calendar/lib/CalendarService.ts:262-264 — removing the console.error block eliminates the only diagnostic for failed Outlook refreshes, and the generic "Invalid refreshed tokens were returned" error loses the actual Microsoft error body, making failures undebuggable

No tests accompany the new app-credential.ts webhook, parseRefreshTokenResponse, or refreshOAuthTokens; a single unit test on minimumTokenResponseSchema or the sync-mode return value would have caught the defects

apps/web/pages/api/webhook/app-credential.ts:23 — Node lowercases request header keys, so a CALCOM_WEBHOOK_HEADER_NAME containing uppercase characters always yields undefined and 403s every request; the lookup should call `.toLowerCase()`

.env.example:240-242 — comment says the key must be 32 bytes for AES256 but the suggested command `openssl rand -base64 24` produces 24 random bytes, contradicting both the comment and the `-base64 32` recommendation three lines above
zoho-bigin/api/add.ts:17 — `${appConfig.slug}` replaced with a hardcoded `zoho-bigin` inside a template literal that now has no interpolation, decoupling the redirect URI from the app config

goldens.comment: The parseRefreshTokenResponse function incorrectly sets refresh_token to the hardcoded string 'refresh_token' when it's missing from the OAuth refresh token response. This invalidates the token, breaking subsequent token refreshes and causing authentication failures.

The Zod schema in parseRefreshTokenResponse uses computed property keys [z.string().toString()] and [z.string().optional().toString()] in minimumTokenResponseSchema, which is invalid Zod syntax and will throw a runtime error.

parseRefreshTokenResponse returns a Zod safeParse result ({ success, data, error }), not the credential key object. Persisting that as key stores the wrapper instead of the token payload; we should store the parsed data or use schema parse.

When APP_CREDENTIAL_SHARING_ENABLED and CALCOM_CREDENTIAL_SYNC_ENDPOINT are set, the refreshFunction helper returns the fetch Response, but several callers (for example GoogleCalendarService.refreshAccessToken expecting res.data, and HubspotCalendarService.refreshAccessToken expecting a HubspotToken) assume it returns the integration-specific token object. That mismatch will cause runtime errors in the sync-enabled path unless the return type or those call sites are adjusted.

When the sync endpoint path is used, res is a fetch Response and has no .data; res?.data will be undefined and token.access_token will throw at runtime. This relies on a consistent return shape from refreshOAuthTokens, which isn’t guaranteed currently.

The `refreshOAuthTokens` function is passed `credentialId` instead of `userId`, which breaks the credential sync functionality by causing incorrect user lookups. This issue can lead to failures in syncing user credentials, impacting user experience.

The Salesforce integration checks `response.statusText` instead of `response.ok` when handling OAuth token refresh responses. This can lead to unreliable behavior, as a successful response may not be correctly identified, resulting in the use of stale credentials and potential authentication failures.

The `jsforce.Connection` is created using stale `credentialKey.access_token` and `credentialKey.instance_url` after a token refresh, which can lead to authentication failures and incorrect data access. Ensure that the connection is established using the refreshed token values instead.

The `appCredentialWebhookRequestBodySchema.parse` function can throw on invalid payloads, resulting in 500 Internal Server Errors instead of the expected 400 Bad Request responses. This can lead to confusion for clients and hinder proper error handling.

adjudication_records.issue_text: apps/web/pages/api/webhook/app-credential.ts:16 — no HTTP method check, so GET/DELETE and other methods fall through to credential mutation, unlike every other handler which gates on method via defaultHandler

adjudication.rationale: The new API route `apps/web/pages/api/webhook/app-credential.ts` exports a handler that never checks `req.method`. After the feature-flag and secret-header checks, it unconditionally parses `req.body` and then performs `prisma.credential.update`/`create`, so any HTTP method (GET/DELETE/etc.) that includes the expected header and body can trigger credential mutation. There is no 405/allow-list gating like typical Next.js handlers that enforce POST-only behavior.

adjudication_records.issue_text: office365calendar/lib/CalendarService.ts:262-264 — removing the console.error block eliminates the only diagnostic for failed Outlook refreshes, and the generic "Invalid refreshed tokens were returned" error loses the actual Microsoft error body, making failures undebuggable

adjudication.rationale: In office365calendar/lib/CalendarService.ts the diff replaces `refreshTokenResponseSchema.safeParse(responseJson)` plus an explicit `console.error(..., tokenResponse.error, ..., responseJson)` on failure with `parseRefreshTokenResponse(responseJson, refreshTokenResponseSchema)`. The new helper throws `new Error("Invalid refreshed tokens were returned")` when parsing fails and does not log/include the Microsoft `responseJson` or Zod error. This verifiably removes the only in-file diagnostic output for schema/refresh failures and replaces it with a generic error message, reducing debuggability.

adjudication_records.issue_text: No tests accompany the new app-credential.ts webhook, parseRefreshTokenResponse, or refreshOAuthTokens; a single unit test on minimumTokenResponseSchema or the sync-mode return value would have caught the defects

adjudication.rationale: The diff indeed adds new functionality (the webhook handler and OAuth helpers) without adding any test files or test changes, so the “no tests accompany” part is factually true. However, the finding does not identify a concrete, verifiable defect in the code itself; it’s a general process/coverage comment and assumes project requirements about tests that are not evidenced in the diff. The claim that a test “would have caught the defects” is also not grounded because it doesn’t specify an actual defect in the diff.

adjudication_records.issue_text: apps/web/pages/api/webhook/app-credential.ts:23 — Node lowercases request header keys, so a CALCOM_WEBHOOK_HEADER_NAME containing uppercase characters always yields undefined and 403s every request; the lookup should call `.toLowerCase()`

adjudication.rationale: In `apps/web/pages/api/webhook/app-credential.ts`, the secret check indexes `req.headers[...]` using `process.env.CALCOM_WEBHOOK_HEADER_NAME` verbatim. In Node/Next.js, incoming header names are normalized to lowercase on `req.headers`, so if the env var is set to any mixed/uppercase value (e.g. `X-Calcom-Secret`), `req.headers["X-Calcom-Secret"]` will be `undefined`, causing the comparison to fail and returning 403 for all requests. The diff even hints at this (“Should be in lowercase”) but the code does not enforce it (e.g., via `.toLowerCase()`).

adjudication_records.issue_text: .env.example:240-242 — comment says the key must be 32 bytes for AES256 but the suggested command `openssl rand -base64 24` produces 24 random bytes, contradicting both the comment and the `-base64 32` recommendation three lines above

adjudication.rationale: In the added .env.example block, the comment for CALCOM_APP_CREDENTIAL_ENCRYPTION_KEY says it “must be 32 bytes for AES256”, but the suggested generation command is `openssl rand -base64 24`. In OpenSSL, the numeric argument to `rand` is the number of random bytes generated before base64 encoding, so `-base64 24` corresponds to 24 bytes (not 32). This is a clear contradiction within the diff’s guidance/comments.
